INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
The Medical Justice Alliance (“MJA”) is a nonprofit
organization with a network of over 940 clinicians and
other healthcare professionals who volunteer their
medical expertise, pro bono, in legal matters involving
incarcerated patients. MJA’s volunteers review medical records and provide written or oral testimony for
attorneys seeking appropriate medical care or compassionate release for their clients. MJA’s volunteer network includes clinicians across 30 different specialties
who are employed by many of the top hospitals and academic institutions across the country. MJA physicians also educate courts, policymakers, clinicians,
and the public about healthcare in carceral settings
and advocate for improved access to care. MJA is
strongly committed to the medical profession and to
ensuring effective medical care for incarcerated persons. MJA’s work gives it a perspective distinct from
that of the parties in this case. Its clinicians have reviewed hundreds of matters involving medical care in
federal custody. That work exposes them to the practical mechanics of obtaining care in prison: how a patient reports symptoms, how records and laboratory
results are reviewed, how referrals are made, how outside treatment is scheduled, and how delays can alter
a patient’s prognosis.
The Medical Justice Alliance-Massachusetts (“MJA-
MA”) is a state chapter of the national Medical Justice
Alliance. MJA-MA is a group of more than 50

2

healthcare providers, social workers, public health researchers, and advocates who care deeply about improving medical care and conditions of confinement for
those incarcerated across the Commonwealth. They
partner with legal advocacy groups, grassroots organizations, and incarcerated people and their loved ones
to seek change through three main avenues of advocacy: Individual and Systemic Advocacy, Legislative
and Policy Advocacy, and Advocacy for the Rights of
Incarcerated People in Hospitals. MJA-MA also runs a
biweekly carceral health case review clinic in which
they advise advocates on the community standard of
care for medical issues that incarcerated people encounter.
The Georgia Human Rights Clinic (“GHRC”) is committed to ensuring all residents of Georgia, regardless
of legal status, have access to basic rights including
but not limited to: healthcare, legal representation,
and personal and family support. This is accomplished
through working with local legal organizations to provide forensic medical evaluations, medical chart reviews, and advocating for adequate medical care in detention facilities. Through grassroots organizing and
collaborations with community partners across the
state, GHRC is committed to ensuring patient rights
are protected and advanced.
The Chicago Medical Legal Collaborative (“CMLC”)
equips clinicians and clinician-learners with the skills,
relationships, and grounding to move between medical
care, legal advocacy, and collective action in defense of
life. Through community-centered forensic work, mentorship, and education, CMLC supports people impacted by social and political forces that disrupt
health. CMLC is building toward a future where this
kind of practice is no longer rare—but a shared stand-

3

ard of how clinicians are trained, supported, and engaged in the world. CMLC is also known as the Chicago People’s Rights Collaborative (“CPRC”).
Stop Criminalization Of Our Patients (“SCOOP”) is
an organization of healthcare and public health workers whose research and education initiatives analyze
the intersections between the criminal legal system
and health. SCOOP’s curricular materials have been
integral to the education of hundreds of medical students and medical residents, informing them about the
complexities of healthcare within jails and prisons as
well as providing best-practice guidance for the care of
in-custody patients in community hospitals and clinics. SCOOP members have cared for dozens of in-custody patients in a hospital-based setting and reviewed
thousands of patient medical records in support of
medical release cases including from the local, state,
and federal system.
Amici submit this brief to explain why the closed nature of prison healthcare, the systemic constraints under which clinicians work in  prisons, and the medical
consequences of delayed or deferred care make the
narrow remedy recognized in Carlson v. Green , 446
U.S. 14 (1980), an importan t accountability backstop
when federal officials are deliberately indifferent to serious medical needs.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Court should affirm the straightforward application of Carlson’s narrow but important accountability function below.
When the government incarcerates a person, it assumes responsibility for and controls all aspects of that
person’s medical care. An incarcerated patient can initiate the process by submitting a sick-call request, but

4

from that point forward has little ability to direct, accelerate, or supplement the course of care. The institution controls when, or if, the patient will be seen,
whether diagnostic testing or medication will be ordered, and whether specialty or hospital care will be
authorized. Unlike a patient outside of prison, an incarcerated patient cannot obtain an earlier appointment from another provider, seek testing or treatment
independently, visit an ur gent-care clinic or emergency department, or choose a different physician or
competing healthcare system. Specialty or hospital
care requires still more institutional action, including
medical review and approval, scheduling with an outside provider, secure transportation, and staff escorts.
Those steps may serve legitimate clinical and security
purposes. But because incarcerated patients cannot
bypass or supplement them, they are at risk of serious
medical consequences from compounding delays that
can impact the entire course of their diagnosis and
treatment.
Amici have witnessed countless cases where delayed
treatment led to emergency surgery, disease progression, and even death. A condition may not be lifethreatening on the day it first appears, but it can become irreversible after months without diagnosis or
proper treatment. Belated care may mitigate injury,
but it cannot restore lost organ function, erase prolonged pain, or reverse the narrowing of treatment options caused by delay. In a system where patients cannot independently seek treatment, Carlson supplies a
narrow but important accountability backstop to deter
unconstitutionally deficient care.
Because respondent’s claim falls squarely within
Carlson’s existing context rather than a new one, the
judgment below should be affirmed.

5

ARGUMENT
I. INCARCERATED PATIENTS ARE WHOLLY
DEPENDENT ON THE FEDERAL PRISON
HEALTHCARE SYSTEM FOR PHYSICAL
MEDICAL CARE.
Incarcerated patients depend on the government for
medical care, cannot obtain substitute care on their
own, and must navigate a sequence of institutional decisions before treatment can occur. Because such patients cannot exit the system, Carlson is essential to
incentivize attention to serious medical needs and reinforce the Eighth Amendment’s constitutional floor.
A. The Governing Legal Framework Reflects the Unique Dependence on Federal
Prison Healthcare Created by Incarceration.
A person outside prison can ordinarily obtain medical care without government permission; a person in
custody cannot. In Estelle v. Gamble, the Court recognized that prisoners must rely on prison authorities to
treat medical needs. 429 U.S. 97, 103–04 (1976). If
prison authorities do not provide that care, the need
may simply go unmet. Id. The Court has repeatedly
found that when confinement prevents a person from
caring for himself or seekin g outside aid, the government assumes responsibility for basic needs, including
medical care. See DeShaney v. Winnebago Cnty. Dep’t
of Soc. Servs., 489 U.S. 189, 199–200 (1989) (explaining that when the government takes a person into custody, “the Constitution imposes upon it a corresponding duty to assume some responsibility for his safety
and general well-being”); see also Farmer v. Brennan,
511 U.S. 825, 833 (1994); Youngberg v. Romeo, 457
U.S. 307, 317 (1982); Brown v. Plata , 563 U.S. 493,
510–11 (2011). That enforced dependence is why the

6

government’s obligation to provide medical care is not
merely aspirational; deliberate indifference to a serious medical need constitutes cruel and unusual punishment where inadequate medical care results in pain
and suffering that serves no penological purpose. Estelle, 429 U.S. at 104.
In Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Fed. Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971), the Court recognized an implied cause of action against federal officials for Fourth Amendment violations. Carlson extended Bivens, holding that federal officials can be
subject to damages for Eighth Amendment violations
where they are deliberately indifferent to a prisoner’s
serious medical needs. 446 U.S. at 18–23. Key to the
Court’s holding was the recognition that it is “almost
axiomatic that the threat of damages has a deterrent
effect” and is essential to remediate unconstitutional
conduct and hold federal officials accountable for inadequate medical care. Id. at 21.
The constitutional standard is demanding. A poor
outcome does not itself show deliberate indifference.
Nor do negligence, medical malpractice, an inadvertent failure to provide adequate care, or a good-faith
disagreement over the proper course of treatment. Estelle, 429 U.S. at 105–07. A plaintiff must show both
an objectively serious and substantial risk of serious
harm and that the official knew of and disregarded
that risk. Farmer, 511 U.S. at 834–37.
This framework creates an essential but narrow accountability mechanism for patients dependent on
prison officials to obtain treatment for serious medical
conditions.

7

B. Prison Healthcare Lacks the Choices and
Incentives That Are Ordinarily Present
in the Healthcare Market.
Carlson serves an essential function because the accountability mechanisms that operate in other
healthcare settings are missing from the prison
healthcare system. See Ira P. Robbins, Managed
Health Care in Prisons as Cruel and Unusual Punishment, 90 J. Crim. L. & Criminology 195, 197 (1999) (explaining that “[c]oncerns regarding inadequate health
care are magnified in a prison setting, in which inmates have no choice about health care and cannot
seek outside advice,” and where prisoners are left to
the discretion of the chosen health care provider).
Outside prison, market forces, including competition, help regulate healthcare systems while promoting higher quality care. See Fed. Trade Comm’n & U.S.
Dep’t of Just., Improving Health Care: A Dose of Competition 4 (2004) (explaining that competition can
broaden access and promote higher quality care). A
community patient who believes that care is inadequate generally has options. The patient may seek a
second opinion, change providers, visit an urgent-care
clinic or emergency department, obtain an independent diagnostic test, obtain at-home care, or leave a
healthcare system that is not responsive. For example,
a second opinion—which is not available to incarcerated patients—can confirm the initial assessment,
identify a different diagno sis or treatment approach,
and provide the patient with additional information
before making consequential healthcare decisions. See
Velma L. Payne et al.,  Patient-Initiated Second Opinions: Systematic Review of Characteristics and Impact
on Diagnosis, Treatment, and Satisfaction , 89 Mayo

8

Clinic Procs. 687, 687 (2014) (finding that 10 to 62 percent of second opinions resulted in a major change in
diagnosis, treatment, or prognosis).
Those options do not guarantee adequate care. But
patient choice and market competition create incentives for healthcare provid ers to improve quality and
lower costs. See U.S. Dep’t of Health & Hum. Servs.,
U.S. Dep’t of Treasury & U.S. Dep’t of Lab., Reforming
America’s Healthcare System Through Choice and
Competition 8 (2018) (explaining that consumer choice
gives firms incentives to improve quality and lower
costs and that, without competitive pressure, incentives to improve quality and innovation diminish).
There are no comparable incentives in the prison
healthcare system. The Federal Bureau of Prisons’
(“BOP”) current Patient Care Program Statement provides that inmates ordinarily may not use non-contracted community providers, including physicians
who treated them before incarceration. See Fed. Bureau of Prisons, U.S. De p’t of Just., Program Statement No. 6031.06, Patient Care § 5(a) (June 22, 2026)
[hereinafter BOP Patient Care Statement]. The institution’s Health Services Unit oversees primary, ancillary, and specialty services delivered on site, through
telehealth, or by contractors. Id. § 2(j). Thus, when
care is delayed or a patient’s condition worsens, the
patient cannot simply schedule an appointment with
another doctor or pay for a different course of treatment. Ordinary market pressures that encourage responsiveness and quality care are entirely absent from
the prison healthcare system.
Incarcerated patients thus must rely on outside
forces to create incentives for the provision of constitutionally adequate care. Carlson is essential among
those forces because the risk of individual liability creates an incentive for prison officials to address known,

9

serious medical risks in a system they know the patient cannot exit.
II. SYSTEMIC CAPACITY LIMITATIONS AND
MULTI-STEP INTERNAL PROCESSES IN-
CREASE THE RISK OF DELAYED DIAGNO-
SIS AND TREATMENT FOR INCARCER-
ATED PATIENTS.
System-wide capacity constraints and a multi-step
internal process can delay care for incarcerated patients, with potentially serious medical consequences.
Staffing shortages, limited specialty care access,
transportation demands, and coordination failures do
not themselves establish deliberate indifference, but
they can create bottlenecks at every stage of the care
pathway and allow a serious condition to worsen before a provider intervenes. Likewise, internal clinical
review procedures can delay diagnosis and treatment
for incarcerated patients. Those structural problems
are not what Carlson remedies—a damages action
cannot add clinicians, expand  diagnostic capacity, or
rewrite BOP’s referral proc edures. Their relevance is
narrower but critical. In a closed system, these constraints increase the importan ce of each official’s response to a known serious risk because the patient
cannot obtain substitute care. Against this backdrop,
Carlson incentivizes attention to the serious medical
risk that delayed care can create and preserves a remedy in the exceptional case when an official knowingly
disregards that risk.
A. System-wide Capacity Constraints Can
Impede and Delay Care.
The federal prison healthcare system has limited resources. Even as BOP has sought and received some
additional resources to address staffing and
healthcare costs, federal prison healthcare continues

10

to face staffing shortages and operational constraints
that can delay routine appointments, diagnostic testing, specialty care, and transportation to outside providers. See Off. of the Inspector Gen., U.S. Dep’t of
Just., Top Management and Performance Challenges
Facing the Department of Justice 2025  2–3, 14–15
(2025) [hereinafter Top Management Report] (describing supplemental funding for hiring employees, including medical professionals, and explaining that addressing long-term staffing shortages will require additional appropriations). The BOP’s own policy recognizes that Health Services staffing varies by institution and that, when vacancies occur, medical leadership must set priorities among intake screenings, comprehensive evaluations, and the sickest patients. See
BOP Patient Care Statement §§ 3(c), 6. In a closed system, such triage can mean that a lower-acuity concern
waits while the institution attends to an emergency.
However, a condition’s acuity may not be known until
an examination, test, or specialist consultation occurs,
and for certain conditions, that delay can be the difference between a treatable diagnosis and a terminal one.
Recent inspections by the Office of the Inspector
General (“OIG”) illustrate these constraints. At Federal Detention Center SeaTac, the OIG found that only
10 of 20 authorized Health Services positions were
filled, while a BOP staffing tool estimated that 40 positions were needed—30 mo re positions than were
filled at the time. Off. of the Inspector Gen., U.S. Dep’t
of Just., Inspection of the Federal Bureau of Prisons’
Federal Detention Center SeaTac , No. 25-081, at 4–7
(Sep. 2025) [hereinafter SeaTac Inspection]. Health
Services leaders reported that they had to prioritize
emergency care over day-to-day health needs. Id. at 3.
Among 29 of the most serious documented sick-call re-

11

quests the OIG reviewed, including complaints of respiratory illness and severe pain, 18 showed no evidence that a healthcare provider had addressed the
complaint. Id. at 6. For the 11 patients who were eventually seen, the average wait was 2.4 months. Id. Outside care presented an additional bottleneck. At
SeaTac, 121 approved outside appointments were
pending; 91 of those approved appointments had not
yet been scheduled and had been pending for an average of 7.4 months. Id. at 7.
At Federal Medical Center Devens, a facility with a
medical mission, the OIG found only 113 of 149 Health
Services positions filled. Off. of the Inspector Gen.,
U.S. Dep’t of Just., Inspection of the Federal Bureau of
Prisons’ Federal Medical Center Devens, No. 25-009, at
i (Dec. 2024) [hereinafter Deve ns Inspection]. It also
found 57 outside appointments that were overdue by
an average of 53 days. Id. at ii. The OIG attributed this
in part to a lack of staff available to escort patients
while maintaining required institutional posts. Id. at
17. These reports reflect a wider trend across BOP facilities. See Top Management Report at 2–3 (identifying staffing shortages and deficiencies in inmate
healthcare as persistent challenges facing BOP). In a
system with limited resources, the referral, scheduling, record transmission, transportation, and staffing
procedures are not abstract  considerations. Each can
determine whether a patient receives adequate and
timely care. See SeaTac Inspection at 7–8; Devens Inspection at 11, 17–18.
These system-wide constr aints therefore provide
context, not a standalone basis for liability. They help
explain why individual accountability remains important when an official is actually aware of a serious
medical risk and the patient lacks an independent
route to care.

12

B. The Prison System’s Multi-step Institutional Process Delays Care And Increases Medical Risks For Incarcerated
Patients.
Incarcerated patients who need medical attention
must navigate a complex institutional process that can
delay diagnosis and treatment, with potentially serious consequences.
Under BOP policy, sick call is the process through
which an inmate initiates a visit for an acute medical
issue. BOP Patient Care Statement § 19. The request
ordinarily must be made in person, assessed and triaged by a qualified provider, and documented in the
electronic health record with the patient’s history, vital signs, examination, and disposition—the decision
about next steps. Id. Urgent conditions are to be
treated expeditiously; non-urgent complaints may be
scheduled for later follow-up or the next chronic-care
clinic. Id. If the same unresolved complaint recurs on
three distinct occasions without a diagnosis or response to treatment, the policy calls for referral to the
Clinical Director or a physician. Id.
Diagnostic and specialty care create additional
handoffs. Routine clinical services, medication administration, testing, and specialty clinics are generally
scheduled through the Health Services Unit. See id.
§ 7(a), (d). Before an outside specialist referral, a physician or other authorized provider ordinarily must review the electronic health record and examine the patient. The request then goes  to the Clinical Director,
another trained clinician, or the Utilization Review
Committee for review and disposition. Id. § 4(e). If approved, the institution or its contractor must locate
and schedule a provider, arrange secure transportation, and assign personnel to escort and supervise the
patient. BOP policy directs facilities to use telehealth

13

when clinically appropriate in part to reduce the staffing and transportation demands associated with outside medical trips. Id. § 29.
The BOP Patient Care Statement does not identify a
fixed deadline for reviewing or completing a non-emergency consultation. An inmate may challenge a delay
through BOP’s general Administrative Remedy Program, but that process ordinarily begins with informal
resolution and may proceed through institutional, regional, and Central Office review. Once a request or
appeal is filed, the regulations allow response periods
of 20, 30, and 40 calendar days at those respective levels, subject to extensio ns. See 28 C.F.R. §§ 542.13–
542.15, 542.18.
None of these bureaucratic steps is inherently problematic. Clinical review helps ensure that referrals are
medically necessary; scheduling and escorts address
legitimate security needs; and coordination with outside providers is unavoidable when a prison does not
offer a specialty on site. Bu t these procedures can impede prompt treatment and diagnosis for serious medical conditions.
For example, a 2025 OIG evaluation of BOP’s colorectal-cancer screening and follow-up practices found
that delays often occurred. Among 133 inmates included in its timeliness analysis, the average interval
between a positive screening and a colonoscopy was
eight months. See Off. of the Inspector Gen., U.S. Dep’t
of Just., Evaluation of the Federal Bureau of Prisons’
Colorectal Cancer Screening Practices for Inmates and
Its Clinical Follow-up on Screenings, No. 25-057, at ii,
24 (May 2025). Only 12 received a colonoscopy within
90 days, and eight waited more than 18 months. Id.
Inmates who first had to complete a separate pre-colonoscopy evaluation waited an average of ten months,
compared with six months for inmates who did not. Id.

14

at 25–26. Both averages substantially exceeded the 90-
day period that community practice generally aims to
meet following a positive screening. Id. at ii, 24.
C. Delays in Diagnosis and Treatment Can
Worsen Disease and Narrow Available
Treatment Options.
Delays in diagnosis and treatment standing alone
will not give rise to a viable claim under Carlson, but
the risk of individual liability incentivizes attention to
the risks that delay can create for an individual patient with serious medical needs. Indeed, many serious
conditions are manageable when detected and treated
promptly. For example, kidney disease may require laboratory monitoring and kidney care before organ
function declines. Cancer treatment depends on early
diagnosis and treatment while meaningful options remain. Respiratory disease may require pulmonary
testing, specialist evaluation, and daily treatment before repeated symptoms become a crisis. In many
cases, delay can change not only a patient’s prognosis
but also the treatment options that remain available.
See, e.g., World Health Org., Guide to Cancer Early Diagnosis 1, 6, 8 (2017) (explaining that cancer identified
early is more likely to re spond to effective and less
complex treatment and may be detected at a potentially curable stage); Linan Cheng et al., Early Versus
Late Nephrology Referral and Patient Outcomes in
Chronic Kidney Disease: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis , 26 BMC Nephrology 1, art.
25, at 1–2 (2025) (finding th at early nephrology referral was associated with fewer emergency dialysis
starts, more kidney transplants, and better preparation for kidney-replacement therapy). The same timing principle applies to physical injuries. A recent systematic review explained that missed physical injuries

15

“remain a significant and potentially preventable complication in trauma care, often associated with increased morbidity, mortality, [and] prolonged hospitalization[.]” Lucas Fontenelle Vieira et al., Missed Injuries in Trauma Care: An Analysis of Mechanisms and
Prevention of One of the Surgeon’s Worst Nightmares,
56 Inj. 112600, 1 (2025).
The acute/chronic distinction does not reliably measure medical seriousness. For example, asthma—the
condition at issue in Carlson—is a chronic disease that
can produce acute or subac ute exacerbations; severe
exacerbations require urgent care and can be fatal
even in people with infrequent baseline symptoms. See
Glob. Initiative for Asthma, Summary Guide for
Asthma Management and Prevention 5–6 (2025). Conversely, an acute traumatic injury can remain a serious medical need when pain persists or the injury remains undiagnosed. Whether a condition presents in
an acute or chronic phase, the medically relevant questions concern the patient’s symptoms, the known risk
of harm, and whether timely evaluation or escalation
is warranted—not the label attached to the condition.
MJA’s clinicians have seen how delays in specialty
evaluation and treatment can affect medical outcomes
in practice. In one matter, a patient with clear signs of
kidney disease did not receive a nephrology consultation—which MJA experts identified as the standard of
care—for months until the patient required multiple
emergency hospitalizations for kidney failure and sepsis. Before being granted compassionate release, the
patient was placed on dialysis and also underwent urgent heart surgery, which carries a higher risk for patients with kidney disease. In another matter, an MJA
physician reviewing records in connection with compassionate-release proceedings identified symptoms
highly concerning for advanced cancer that had not

16

been acted upon; the patient died before the court
ruled. In a third, a patient with chronic respiratory
symptoms and a family history of COPD, asthma, and
lung cancer, had not been referred to a pulmonologist
until an MJA physician reviewed the records and recommended specialty care; the patient was then released to pursue evaluation and treatment in the community. MJA’s materials do not identify whether these
delays resulted from staffi ng shortages, referral or
scheduling failures, limited diagnostic capacity, or
other causes. These examples therefore are not offered
to attribute the delays to an y particular constraint or
clinician; they illustrate the medical consequences
when an incarcerated patient does not receive timely
specialty review. See Med. Just. All., Public Comment
on 88 Fed. Reg. 7180 Proposed Amendment No. 1, at 3–
4 (Mar. 14, 2023).
When the institution controls the patient’s only
route to testing, specialty care, and treatment, an unaddressed warning sign or delayed referral can allow
a manageable condition to become an emergency before prospective relief can help. Carlson preserves a
remedy for the exceptional case in which an official
knowingly disregards that serious medical risk, while
leaving negligence and good-faith clinical judgment
outside constitutional liability.
III. CARLSON PROVIDES AN IMPORTANT,
BUT LIMITED, ACCOUNTABILITY MECHA-
NISM WHEN SERIOUS MEDICAL NEEDS
ARE MET WITH DELIBERATE INDIFFER-
ENCE.
Carlson provides a narrow remedy for violations of a
prisoner’s right to adequate medical care. Individual
liability creates incentives to address known, serious
medical risks in a system the patient cannot exit, while
the demanding deliberate-indifference standard

17

leaves negligence, malpractice, and good-faith clinical
judgment or disagreement outside constitutional liability.
A. Carlson Supplies a Limited Accountability Mechanism Where Ordinary
Healthcare Incentives Are Absent.
Carlson made plain that a Bivens remedy, in addition to compensating a person who has been injured,
serves a crucial deterrent purpose. 446 U.S. at 20–21.
The Court later reiterated that point in Correctional
Services Corp. v. Malesko: “the purpose of Bivens is to
deter individual federal officers from committing constitutional violations[,]” an d “the threat of litigation
and liability” provides that  deterrence even when an
officer may be indemnified or may assert qualified immunity. 534 U.S. 61, 70–71 (2001).
Carlson also anticipated that the potential for individual liability could influence institutional practice.
In rejecting the argument that only liability against
the United States would prompt corrective policies,
the Court reasoned that responsible supervisors would
likewise respond when an employee is found personally liable for violating cons titutional rights. 446 U.S.
at 21 (“[R]esponsible superiors are motivated not only
by concern for the public fi sc but also by concern for
the Government’s integrity.”). That response has been
observed in practice. In a national survey of 27 state
prison systems and 44 larg e jails, approximately 70
percent of respondents in each group reported changing policies, procedures, or practices as a result of individual inmate lawsuits. Margo Schlanger, Inmate
Litigation: Results of a National Survey, LJN Exch. 1,
1, 8–9 (2003). Medical and me ntal-health care were
the most common subjects of the substantive operational changes respondents identified. Id.

18

Schlanger’s corrections-focused research identifies
concrete mechanisms for that response. She reports
that correctional systems facing recurring litigation
create incident reports, vi deotape cell extractions,
maintain shift logs, adopt written policies, and develop
procedures that allow supervisors to monitor line staff.
See Margo Schlanger, Inmate Litigation, 116 Harv. L.
Rev. 1555, 1666–68 (2003). More broadly, Schlanger
concluded that inmate litigation has a “beneficial, if
limited, tendency to encourage [correctional] agencies
to comply with constitutional norms” and can prompt
operational changes extending beyond the defense of
any particular lawsuit. Id. at 1668. She also found that
several large damages verdicts against the Federal
Bureau of Prisons involving inmate suicides
“prompted high-level review of suicide-prevention policies and practices.” Id. at 1677–83. Schlanger’s later
work describes how claims-management personnel
can translate liability signals into changes in information gathering, specialized compliance functions,
and operating practices. See Margo Schlanger, Operationalizing Deterrence: Claims Management (In Hospitals, a Large Retailer, and Jails and Prisons), 2 J. Tort
L. 1, art. 1, at 44–49 (2008) . Those effects are not automatic, and amici do not contend that every suit
changes institutional behavior. But a credible possibility of individual accountability can give the constitutional standard practical force.
That force is especially important in a closed
healthcare system. Because incarcerated patients cannot obtain substitute care, an accountability mechanism can reinforce attention to serious complaints,
contemporaneous documentation of clinical decisions,
review of worsening symptoms, and timely escalation
when a known risk warrants it.

19

B. The Demanding Standard Protects Legitimate Medical Judgment.
The demanding deliberate-indifference standard
protects legitimate medical judgment, including difficult triage and treatment decisions made under constrained conditions. Systemic limitations may impede
care even when clinicians act in good faith; constitutional liability arises only when an official knowingly
disregards a substantial risk of serious harm. The
standard therefore preserves room for reasonable clinical judgment while reaching exceptional constitutional violations.
Petitioner argues that Carlson  liability may incentivize prison clinicians to act defensively by ordering
unnecessary tests or hospital  transfers. Pet. Br. 29.
But the article petitioner ci tes does not support that
extrapolation; the article studies state-law medicalmalpractice liability and to rt reform among elderly
Medicare patients with serious heart disease, not
prison healthcare or liability under the far more demanding constitutional deliberate-indifference standard. See Daniel P. Kessler & Mark McClellan, Do Doctors Practice Defensive Medicine?, 111 Q. J. Econ. 353
(1996).
Thus, petitioner’s concern misses the standard amici
defend. Deliberate indifference does not impose liability for declining medically unnecessary care, choosing
among reasonable diagnostic options, or making a
good-faith triage decision; an official who responds
reasonably to a known risk is not liable even if the
harm is not ultimately averted. See Farmer, 511 U.S.
at 844. From a clinician’s perspective, the line is familiar: reasonable medical judgment remains protected,
while conscious disregard of a known serious risk does
not. Carlson therefore encourages attention to red

20

flags and timely escalati on when clinically warranted—not indiscriminate testing or automatic hospital transfer.
Estelle expressly distinguished deliberate indifference from negligence and malpractice. 429 U.S. at
105–06. And Farmer requires proof that an official was
aware of facts supporting an inference of a substantial
risk, actually drew that inference, and nevertheless
disregarded the risk. 511 U.S. at 837. A patient cannot
prevail merely by showing that a different test should
have been ordered, that a specialist would have selected another treatment, or that care did not produce
the desired outcome.
That distinction matters for clinicians working under pressure. Medicine often involves uncertainty, triage, and competing reasonable approaches. Carlson
does not authorize courts to replace clinical judgment
with hindsight. It applies only after a plaintiff proves
a serious need and culpable state of mind. Preserving
this existing remedy therefore does not expose providers to liability for every delay or adverse result; it preserves accountability for conscious disregard of a serious medical need.
CONCLUSION
This Court should affirm the judgment of the Ninth
Circuit.
